text:
This section examines Chapter 2 — prism’s
evolutionary loop (7–8

minutes) from first principles. Keep two
questions separate: does changing

the order change the measured outcome, and
does the proposed

search method beat a matched alternative
at the same distinct-evaluation

budget? Animate one complete generation
with a small population of

five permutations before showing the full
baseline settings. Explain every

step: Sample mu random permutations.
Decode each ordering into a

system. Evaluate fitness. Copy the global
best into the next

population. Sample k competitors and
select the highest-fitness parent.

Mutate the parent with probability p_m.
Repeat until the next

population is full. Stop after T
generations or an evaluation

budget. Explain the baseline parameters
and their intended role: population

mu=20 for the historical small problems;
tournament size k=3; mutation

probability p_m=0.05; one elite copy; no
crossover, to isolate ordering

and neighborhood effects. Then show how
later experiments altered the

historical settings for harder nge7
landscapes and why distinct evaluated

permutations, not generations alone,
became the cost unit. Include a

line-by-line animation of the three paper
algorithms: main loop, tournament

selection, and generic mutation. Do not
display the entire pseudocode

at once. The distinction is part of the
result. A

large ordering effect does not
automatically imply an evolutionary-search

advantage, and almost-sure convergence
does not promise practical
efficiency.
